title: Best Way to Store a Bread Lame Safely in a Kitchen Drawer
keyword: how to store bread lame safely
meta_description: Learn the best way to store a bread lame safely in a kitchen drawer, protect the blade, and keep your scoring tool ready for every bake.
html:
When you’re serious about sourdough, the bread scoring lame is as essential as the starter itself. But a sharp blade can be a kitchen hazard if it’s not stored correctly. Knowing how to store bread lame safely protects both your fingers and the tool, ensuring a clean cut every time you score a loaf.

Why Proper Storage Matters

Unlike a regular kitchen knife, a lame’s blade is thin, razor‑sharp, and often only a few inches long. A slip in the drawer can nick a finger, damage the edge, or even cause the blade to snap if it hits a hard object. Proper storage also prevents rust, which can ruin the score line and make cleaning a chore.

Choose the Right Drawer Space

Start by designating a specific compartment for your scoring tools. A shallow drawer near the oven or prep area works best because you’ll reach for the lame often. Keep the blade away from bulky items like pots, spatulas, or metal utensils that could knock it around.

Protect the Blade with a Sleeve or Sheath

Most lames come with a protective plastic or leather sheath. If yours didn’t, invest in a small kitchen‑tool sheath—think of it like a pocket for a pocketknife. Slip the blade into the sheath before placing it in the drawer; this simple step eliminates the risk of accidental cuts and preserves the edge.

  • Sheath material: plastic for easy cleaning, leather for a premium feel.
  • Fit: the sheath should snugly hug the blade without wobbling.
  • Accessibility: choose a sheath that slides out quickly so you don’t waste time during a bake.

Use a Dedicated Container or Organizer

If you own a Sourdough Whisk Set, you already have a compact, purpose‑built kit that includes a whisk, scraper, and lame. The set’s packaging can double as a drawer organizer. Place the lame in its own slot, separate from the whisk and scraper, to avoid blade contact with metal surfaces. A small, reusable silicone tray works just as well—just line it with a soft cloth to add extra cushioning.

Maintain a Dry Environment

Moisture is the enemy of a clean blade. After each use, wipe the lame dry with a lint‑free cloth, then lightly oil the edge with a food‑safe oil (vegetable or a drop of neutral olive oil). The oil creates a barrier against humidity and reduces the chance of rust forming while the tool sits in the drawer.

Routine Checks and Blade Care

Even with perfect storage, a blade can dull over time. Every few bakes, inspect the lame for nicks or rust. If you notice any, sharpen it with a fine‑grit sharpening stone or have it professionally honed. A sharp blade not only scores beautifully but also requires less pressure, reducing the chance of slipping.

Putting It All Together: Step‑by‑Step Storage Routine

  1. After scoring, brush off any dough residue with a soft brush.
  2. Wipe the blade dry with a clean, lint‑free towel.
  3. Apply a thin coat of food‑safe oil to the edge.
  4. Slide the blade into its protective sheath.
  5. Place the sheathed lame in its dedicated slot within the drawer organizer (or the compartment of the Sourdough Whisk Set).
  6. Close the drawer gently—no need to slam it shut.

Following this routine takes less than a minute but pays off in safety and performance.

Bonus Tip: Keep a Backup Lame

If you bake frequently, consider buying a second lame. Store the backup in a separate part of the drawer or in a small zip‑top bag. This way, you always have a clean, sharp blade ready, and you avoid the temptation to reuse a dull or damaged tool.

FAQ

Can I store a lame without a sheath?

Yes, but it increases the risk of cuts and edge damage. If you must, wrap the blade in a clean kitchen towel and place it in a dedicated slot away from metal utensils.

Is oiling the blade really necessary?

Oiling creates a protective barrier against moisture, which helps prevent rust. It’s a quick step that extends the lifespan of your lame.

How often should I sharpen my lame?

Inspect the blade after every 5–7 loaves. If the score line looks ragged or you need to press harder, it’s time to hone the edge.
